title: Professional Error Handling
readme:
FULL-STACK DEVELOPER 2026
Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

This phase continues Phase 12's validated persistent Task API.
It introduces a stable API error envelope, Fastify request correlation, NestJS 12 structured logging, a global exception filter, safe Prisma 7 error translation, and frontend error consumption.

Course locks remain:
- NestJS 12.0.3
- Fastify 5.x course line
- Prisma 7.9.1
- Zod 4.6.5

Start with 00_Phase_13_Guide.pdf or read 11_Phase_13_Complete_Book.pdf.
The reference snapshot contains Phase 13 changed files and assumes the Phase 12 project already exists.

lessons.body:
Error Taxonomy & API Contract
Expected failures, unexpected faults, HTTP semantics, machine codes, and public
error design

Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
Failure occurs

↓

Classify meaning

↓

Choose safe status/code

↓

Return stable contract

Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs.

Not every failure is the same
Professional error handling begins by classifying failures before choosing a status code or message. Treating
every exception as a generic 500 makes the API hard to use. Treating every failure as a client mistake hides
real server faults.

Category                        Example                                                Expected handling

Invalid request                 blank title, malformed UUID                            400 with validation details

Missing resource                valid Task ID does not exist                           404 with domain code

State conflict                  duplicate unique value / relation conflict             409

Authentication later            missing/invalid token                                  401

Authorization later             identity lacks permission                              403

Unexpected fault                bug, unavailable dependency, unknown exception         500 sanitized to client

Figure 1 - Expected failure vs unexpected fault
Request enters system

↓

Can the application explain the failure safely?

↓

Yes -> stable 4xx response

↓

No -> log diagnostics internally

↓

Return sanitized 500

A client-facing API should expose actionable contract information without exposing server internals.

Status code is not the whole contract
Two 404 responses can mean different application situations. A stable application error code lets clients
distinguish them without parsing English text.

{
"statusCode": 404,
"code": "TASK_NOT_FOUND",
"message": "Task ... was not found.",
"requestId": "7",
"timestamp": "2026-09-18T...Z",
"path": "/tasks/..."
}

Human message vs machine code

Field                                Purpose

statusCode                           HTTP semantics; proxies, clients and tooling understand it

code                                 Stable machine-readable application meaning

message                              Human-readable explanation

details                              Optional structured validation information

requestId                            Correlation between client failure and server log

timestamp                            When the server produced the error

path                                 Which endpoint failed

Do not parse English messages

Frontend code should branch on statusCode or code, not on exact English wording such as message.includes("not
found"). Messages can change for clarity; stable codes are the contract.

Error handling is a boundary concern
Business services should explain domain failures. The global exception boundary should format those failures
for HTTP. Database adapters should not dictate the public API. This separation prevents infrastructure-specific
error text from becoming a client contract.

lessons.summary: NestJS Exception Layer & Request Lifecycle How filters fit into NestJS 12 request processing and why global error boundaries beat repetitive try/catch Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone request ↓ guards/interceptors/pipes ↓ controller/service ↓ uncaught exception ↓ filter…
lessons.body:
NestJS Exception Layer & Request
Lifecycle
How filters fit into NestJS 12 request processing and why global error boundaries beat
repetitive try/catch

Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
request

↓

guards/interceptors/pipes

↓

controller/service

↓

uncaught exception

↓

filter

↓

response

Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs.

NestJS already has an exception layer
Nest catches unhandled exceptions after request processing and converts HttpException subclasses into
HTTP responses. Unknown errors become a generic 500. Exception filters exist when an application needs
more control over response shape, logging, or error translation.

Figure 1 - Relevant request lifecycle
Incoming request

↓

middleware

↓

guards

↓

interceptors (before)

↓

pipes / validation

↓

controller

↓

service

↓

interceptors (after)

↓

exception filters when an uncaught exception occurs

↓

HTTP response

The filter is the final HTTP error boundary for exceptions that were not already handled.

Why not try/catch every controller?
• Controllers become repetitive and harder to read.

• Validation errors happen before many controller handlers run.

• Infrastructure errors can escape from deeper providers.

• Response formatting drifts between endpoints.

• A global filter centralizes HTTP error serialization without forcing all business logic into the filter.

HttpException is already useful

NestJS exceptions such as BadRequestException, NotFoundException, ConflictException,
UnauthorizedException, and ForbiddenException communicate HTTP intent. TaskFlow keeps using those
concepts, but enriches selected exceptions with stable application codes.

throw new NotFoundException({
code: "TASK_NOT_FOUND",
message: `Task ${taskId} was not found.`,
});

Catch everything - carefully
A @Catch() filter can normalize both known and unknown errors. The filter must not accidentally expose stack
traces, SQL, credentials, or raw Prisma messages to clients. Unknown faults should be logged internally and
returned as a generic 500 response.

Fastify-friendly implementation

NestJS documents a platform-agnostic catch-all filter using HttpAdapterHost. TaskFlow follows that pattern instead
of calling Express response.json(), so the code remains correct with the Fastify adapter selected earlier in the
course.

Global registration through dependency injection
Because our filter needs HttpAdapterHost and our interceptor needs Logger behavior, register them as
APP_FILTER / APP_INTERCEPTOR providers rather than manually creating ad-hoc instances throughout
controllers.

providers: [
{
provide: APP_INTERCEPTOR,
useClass: RequestLoggingInterceptor,
},
{
provide: APP_FILTER,
useClass: ApiExceptionFilter,
},
]

lessons.summary: Design the TaskFlow Error Envelope statusCode, code, message, details, requestId, timestamp, and path Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone failure ↓ normalized API error ↓ client + support correlation Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a…
lessons.body:
Design the TaskFlow Error Envelope
statusCode, code, message, details, requestId, timestamp, and path

Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
failure

↓

normalized API error

↓

client + support correlation

Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs.

Design the TaskFlow error envelope
The API now needs a format that is useful to browser code, PowerShell tests, future mobile clients, and
production logs. Keep it small. Every field should answer a real debugging or client-handling question.

export type ApiErrorDetails = string[] | Record<string, unknown>;

export type ApiErrorResponse = {
statusCode: number;
code: string;
message: string;
requestId: string;
timestamp: string;
path: string;
details?: ApiErrorDetails;
};

Examples by failure type
// 400 validation
{
"statusCode": 400,
"code": "BAD_REQUEST",
"message": "Request validation failed.",
"details": ["title: String must contain at least 1 character(s)"],
"requestId": "12",
"timestamp": "...",
"path": "/tasks"
}

// 404 domain failure
{
"statusCode": 404,
"code": "TASK_NOT_FOUND",
"message": "Task 123... was not found.",
"requestId": "13",
"timestamp": "...",
"path": "/tasks/123..."
}

// 500 unexpected fault
{
"statusCode": 500,
"code": "INTERNAL_ERROR",
"message": "An unexpected server error occurred.",
"requestId": "14",
"timestamp": "...",
"path": "/tasks"
}

Why requestId belongs in the client response
When a user reports a failure, “it broke at 2:13 AM” is weak evidence. A request identifier gives support and
engineering teams an exact correlation key that can be searched in server logs.

Figure 1 - Correlation workflow
Client receives requestId = 14

↓

Support includes 14 in bug report

↓

Engineer searches structured logs for requestId 14

↓

Server log shows method, path, status, exception context

A correlation identifier connects a sanitized public response to private server diagnostics without exposing those diagnostics.

Do not overstuff the contract
Avoid sending implementation fields such as Prisma stack, database host, migration name, SQL statement,
source file path, or environment variable values. They belong in protected logs, not the public transport
contract.

lessons.summary: Prisma Error Translation Translate Prisma 7 P2002, P2003, and P2025 without leaking ORM internals Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Prisma error ↓ domain context if available ↓ safe HTTP mapping Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary…
lessons.body:
Prisma Error Translation
Translate Prisma 7 P2002, P2003, and P2025 without leaking ORM internals

Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
Prisma error

↓

domain context if available

↓

safe HTTP mapping

Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs.

Translate Prisma errors deliberately
Prisma errors are implementation details. Clients should receive HTTP/domain semantics, not raw ORM error
text. TaskFlow catches a small set of understood Prisma 7 codes and gives them stable meanings.

Prisma code              Meaning                                              TaskFlow HTTP mapping

P2002                    Unique constraint failed                             409 UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT

P2003                    Foreign key constraint failed                        409 RELATION_CONFLICT

P2025                    Required record for operation not found              404 RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND

Other known              Known Prisma failure not explicitly modeled          500 DATABASE_ERROR
request error

Do not return Prisma message directly
// BAD public response
{
"message": "Invalid this.prisma.task.create() invocation ...
Unique constraint failed ..."
}

Sensitive implementation detail

Raw ORM messages may contain model names, operation context, field names, local paths, or other details that
clients do not need. Log what engineers need privately; expose a safe contract publicly.

Where P2025 should be handled
For a Task update/delete, the service knows the domain context and can produce TASK_NOT_FOUND. That
is more useful than allowing the global filter to produce generic RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND. The global P2025
mapping remains a safety net for errors that escape from less contextual code.

Figure 1 - Context first, global fallback second
TasksService catches expected P2025

↓

Throws TaskNotFoundException with TASK_NOT_FOUND

↓

Global filter only formats the exception

↓

Unexpected uncaught P2025 elsewhere

↓

Global filter returns generic RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND

Translate errors as close as possible to the layer that understands their business meaning, while keeping a global safety boundary.

Conflict does not always mean 409
Use 409 when the request is structurally valid but conflicts with current server state. Do not mechanically map
every database exception to 409. Connection failures, malformed schema, timeouts, and unknown database
faults are server-side operational failures, not client conflicts.

lessons.summary: Safe Production Error Exposure Sanitized client responses, protected diagnostics, logging hygiene, and privacy-aware failure handling Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone client-safe response ↓ requestId ↓ private structured diagnostic log Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and…
lessons.body:
Safe Production Error Exposure
Sanitized client responses, protected diagnostics, logging hygiene, and privacy-aware
failure handling

Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
client-safe response

↓

requestId

↓

private structured diagnostic log

Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs.

Production errors should be boring to clients and rich
to engineers
The client needs a safe message, stable code, and requestId. Engineers need internal context such as
exception name, stack, method, path, status, and timing. These are different audiences.

Information                                     Public response    Protected server log

status / code                                   Yes                Yes

human-safe message                              Yes                Yes

requestId                                       Yes                Yes

stack trace                                     No                 Yes for unexpected faults

raw SQL                                         No                 Usually no; only under controlled diagnostics

DATABASE_URL / credentials                      Never              Never

request password/token                          Never              Never

Prisma raw error text                           Usually no         May be logged carefully if sanitized

Structured logging example
this.logger.error("Unhandled request failure", {
requestId,
method: request.method,
path,
statusCode: 500,
exceptionName: exception.name,
stack: exception.stack,
});

Do not log request bodies by default
Bodies can contain passwords, tokens, personal data, payroll values, applicant information, employee records,
or uploaded document metadata in future TaskFlow-derived systems. Logging everything because it is
convenient is not professional observability.

Security and privacy rule

Error handling is also data-handling design. Decide what logs are allowed to contain before production, who can
read them, and how long they are retained.

Unknown 500 workflow
Figure 1 - Safe 500 lifecycle
Unexpected exception occurs

↓

Filter creates INTERNAL_ERROR response

↓

Client receives requestId

↓

Server logs requestId + private diagnostic context

↓

Engineer correlates without exposing internals

A secure system does not need to choose between debuggability and safe client responses.

Hands-On Lab & Phase Exit
Error matrix, correlation exercise, engineering challenges, oral exam, and completion
checklist

Phase 13 - Professional Error Handling
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone
implement

↓

trigger errors

↓

correlate logs

↓

verify contract

↓

explain architecture

Phase 13 creates one professional exception boundary and a correlation story that spans client response and server logs.

Hands-on lab
The exit lab proves that TaskFlow has one coherent error boundary instead of a collection of framework-default
responses.

Lab A - Add the error contract
• Create ApiErrorResponse.

• Add TaskNotFoundException and ProjectNotFoundException.

• Update TasksService to throw domain-specific exceptions where context is known.

• Keep unknown exceptions re-thrown.

Lab B - Add global filter and request logging
• Create ApiExceptionFilter using HttpAdapterHost.

• Create RequestLoggingInterceptor using Fastify request.id.

• Register both globally with APP_FILTER and APP_INTERCEPTOR.

• Verify successful responses expose x-request-id.

• Verify 4xx/5xx error bodies contain requestId.

Lab C - Error matrix
Scenario                                                          Expected

GET /tasks/not-a-uuid                                             400 BAD_REQUEST, requestId

GET valid missing Task UUID                                       404 TASK_NOT_FOUND, requestId

POST missing/invalid body                                         400 BAD_REQUEST + details

POST valid body, missing Project                                  404 PROJECT_NOT_FOUND

Known unique conflict (where available)                           409 UNIQUE_CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT

P2025 escaping contextual service handling                        404 RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND fallback

Deliberate unexpected Error in dev test route                     500 INTERNAL_ERROR, no stack in response

Lab D - Correlation exercise
• Trigger one failing request.

• Copy requestId from the JSON response.

• Find the matching NestJS log entry.

• Confirm the client response is sanitized while the log has diagnostic context.

• Remove any temporary route used to create an artificial 500.

Exercise levels
Level                     Challenge

1 - Follow                Implement the reference filter/interceptor and pass the smoke-test matrix.

Level                     Challenge

2 - Modify                Add a stable PROJECT_NOT_FOUND client handling branch in the Next.js API helper demo.

3 - Implement             Add a Task title uniqueness rule inside one Project and map its P2002 conflict safely.

4 - Engineer              Design an error-code naming convention for a future HRIS with payroll, leave, recruitment, and employee
domains; explain which codes are public contracts and which diagnostics remain internal.

Architecture oral exam
• Why should a global error filter not contain Task business rules?

• Why is requestId useful if the client never sees a stack trace?

• When should a service catch a Prisma error instead of relying on the global filter?

• Why is P2002 usually 409 but an unavailable database usually 500?

• What is the difference between a network failure and an API error response?

• Which data should never be written to logs even during debugging?

Phase exit checklist
• all error responses have statusCode, code, message, requestId, timestamp, and path.

• validation details remain useful without exposing internals.

• Task/Project not-found failures have domain codes.

• known Prisma conflicts are translated safely.

• unknown errors return sanitized 500 responses.

• requestId correlates client response and server logs.

• successful responses expose x-request-id.

• NestJS production build passes.

• you can explain which layer owns classification, translation, formatting, and logging.

Figure 1 - Phase 13 complete architecture
Request / Fastify request.id

↓

Validation + Controller + Service

↓

Known domain or infrastructure exception

↓

ApiExceptionFilter

↓

Stable ApiErrorResponse + requestId

↓

Structured server log

TaskFlow now has a professional error boundary that remains useful as authentication, authorization, and business rules become
more complex.

Next phase

Phase 14 will deepen Service & Business Logic Architecture: application invariants, cross-model rules, workflow
methods, transactions where needed, orchestration vs persistence, and keeping controllers thin without turning
services into giant “god classes.”

Guided Build Lab — Phase 13: Professional Error Handling

Purpose
Create a stable application error model that separates expected domain/transport failures from unexpected faults and keeps diagnostics observable.

Deliverable
Error taxonomy + NestJS mapping layer/filters + structured error response with request IDs.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
failure occurs -> typed/application error -> exception mapping -> structured log -> safe HTTP error -> frontend recovery

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Inventory current TaskFlow failures and group them into validation, auth, forbidden, missing, conflict, infrastructure, and unexpected categories.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Create explicit application errors for expected business outcomes rather than throwing arbitrary strings.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Map errors to one stable HTTP envelope at a central boundary.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Step 6 — Prove an unexpected exception returns a generic 500 while the real stack/context remains in logs.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 13: Professional Error Handling

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
failure occurs -> typed/application error -> exception mapping -> structured log -> safe HTTP error -> frontend recovery

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Returning raw exception messages/stacks
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Catching everything inside each controller
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Using one generic 400 for semantically different failures
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — Logging secrets/tokens with error context
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.title: Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge
lessons.summary:
Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 13 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?
lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Professional Error Handling

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 13 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Create a stable application error model that separates expected domain/transport failures from unexpected faults and keeps diagnostics observable.

Required artifact
Error taxonomy + NestJS mapping layer/filters + structured error response with request IDs.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can distinguish expected vs unexpected errors.
• Can map failures centrally.
• Can trace a request by ID.
• Can design frontend recovery from stable error codes.

Independent build sequence
1. Inventory current TaskFlow failures and group them into validation, auth, forbidden, missing, conflict, infrastructure, and unexpected categories.
2. Create explicit application errors for expected business outcomes rather than throwing arbitrary strings.
3. Map errors to one stable HTTP envelope at a central boundary.
4. Add request/correlation IDs to responses and logs.
5. Trigger each error class intentionally and verify both client-safe response and server diagnostic context.
6. Prove an unexpected exception returns a generic 500 while the real stack/context remains in logs.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Inspect the boundary-specific evidence: terminal output, Network panel, database row/query plan, test report, container health, or deployment logs.
Repeat the behavior once after the change so a one-off cached or stale result cannot masquerade as success.
breakIt: Returning raw exception messages/stacks
Change one assumption in the errors example—identity, input, configuration, ordering, connectivity, or state—and predict the exact symptom before running it.

troubleshooting.investigation: Return to the nearest observable boundary: input, network, process log, database, or rendered UI. Compare actual evidence with the predicted path.

troubleshooting.symptom: A shortcut appears to fix it
troubleshooting.investigation: Change one variable at a time and reproduce the original failure after the fix; otherwise you have correlation, not diagnosis.

workshop.challenge: Without copying the final source, create a second small scenario that applies “Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge” to a different TaskFlow resource or input. Write the acceptance criteria first, implement it, and provide the evidence that each criterion is satisfied.
review: What problem does Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge solve in TaskFlow, and what would be observably wrong without it?
Which part of the errors boundary owns the decision, and which neighboring layer must not own it?
What evidence proves the happy path instead of merely suggesting it worked?
Name one realistic failure or abuse case and the first place you would inspect.
If requirements doubled tomorrow, which part of this design should stay stable and which part is allowed to change?

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 13 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 13: Professional Error Handling. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Error taxonomy + NestJS mapping layer/filters + structured error response with request IDs.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

objectives: Create a stable application error model that separates expected domain/transport failures from unexpected faults and keeps diagnostics observable.
Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.
Defend the architecture and identify one improvement without overengineering.
workshop.why: A guided lesson proves you can follow. A capstone proves you can transfer the model to a requirement with fewer cues.
steps: Inventory current TaskFlow failures and group them into validation, auth, forbidden, missing, conflict, infrastructure, and unexpected categories.
Create explicit application errors for expected business outcomes rather than throwing arbitrary strings.
Map errors to one stable HTTP envelope at a central boundary.
Add request/correlation IDs to responses and logs.
Trigger each error class intentionally and verify both client-safe response and server diagnostic context.
Prove an unexpected exception returns a generic 500 while the real stack/context remains in logs.
Run the phase mastery checklist without looking at the provided implementation.
Perform a short architecture review and document one trade-off you consciously accepted.

example.caption: Capstone evidence packet
example.code: Requirement -> implementation diff -> verification -> controlled failure -> diagnosis -> final proof

verify: Can distinguish expected vs unexpected errors
Can map failures centrally
Can trace a request by ID
Can design frontend recovery from stable error codes
breakIt: Returning raw exception messages/stacks
Catching everything inside each controller

troubleshooting.symptom: You can only continue by copying the reference
troubleshooting.investigation: Return to the mental model and acceptance criteria. Rebuild one smaller slice from first principles before reopening the source.

troubleshooting.symptom: Everything seems to work but proof is weak
troubleshooting.investigation: Choose an external observer: HTTP client, browser, database query, test runner, health endpoint, or deployment log, and capture deterministic evidence.

workshop.challenge: Extend the phase artifact with one requirement not used in the guided example while preserving the same ownership rules and verification strategy.
review: What did you build without a transcript?
Which boundary caused the most reasoning effort?
Which failure gave the strongest evidence?
What shortcut did you deliberately avoid?
What would you automate before repeating this in a team?
